report.summary: A LessWrong linkpost asks how the US and China could credibly verify a mutual slowdown of frontier AI development, examining compute tracking, inspections, and treaty design.
report.background: The US and China are the two leading AI powers, yet they have almost no bilateral arms-control framework for AI. Existing policy has leaned on unilateral levers, chiefly US export controls on advanced chips and bilateral talks such as the 2024 Geneva AI dialogue, plus multilateral summit declarations. The verification problem is what separates a serious slowdown agreement from a communiqué: nuclear treaties rely on satellites, on-site inspections, and the IAEA because fissile material is physical and countable, while frontier AI capability is largely software, reproducible in ordinary datacenters, and easy to conceal. The essay (hosted on josefely.substack.com; the LessWrong page is a linkpost) sits in a growing 'compute governance' literature arguing that AI chips are the one scarce, traceable input — making them the natural anchor for any verifiable regime, alongside training-run disclosure, hardware telemetry, and mutual inspection. It also reflects a wider 2025-26 shift from abstract AI-safety warnings toward concrete institutional mechanics.
key_points: Verification is the bottleneck, not intent. Both governments may privately worry about racing, but a deal is worthless if cheating is undetectable. AI is harder to verify than nuclear weapons because frontier training is mostly software and data, leaves few physical signatures, and can be hidden inside commercial cloud infrastructure that already exists.

Compute is the most promising chokepoint. Advanced AI chips are manufactured by a handful of firms, are physically large and serialized, and consume distinctive amounts of power. Proposals therefore center on chip registries, know-your-customer rules, datacenter monitoring, and export-control-style tracking as the backbone of any verification regime.

Concrete mechanisms on the table include training-run reporting above compute thresholds, tamper-evident hardware or remote telemetry, on-site inspections of large datacenters, and mutual confidence-building measures such as shared safety evaluations and incident hotlines — steps that fall short of a formal treaty but build trust and detection capability.

Institutional design is contested. Options range from a bilateral commission and a third-party secretariat modeled on the IAEA to purely unilateral, domestically legislated transparency. Each trades off intrusiveness against political survivability, and each side's domestic politics sharply limit how much inspection the other can be granted.

Enforcement and definitions matter as much as detection. Any slowdown needs a shared definition of 'frontier' that does not freeze out laggards, plus consequences for defection, and must compete with strong economic and military incentives to defect — especially if the agreement is asymmetric or slow to verify.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this debate signals that the policy frontier is moving from export controls toward monitoring obligations: large training runs may eventually carry reporting, licensing, or audit burdens, and hyperscalers could become de facto verification intermediaries. Developers should expect compliance to become a design consideration rather than an afterthought, and startups may face reporting thresholds that entrench incumbents. For regular users, a verified slowdown could mean slower capability releases but more predictable safety practices — or, if verification fails, a continued race with thinner safety margins. For the wider governance field, the essay's value is framing verification as an engineering problem with tractable pieces (chips, power, telemetry) rather than an all-or-nothing treaty question, which makes incremental, testable regimes much more plausible.
